It’s important that everyone is aware of the simple steps they can take to stay safe during periods of hot weather. Drinking plenty of water, avoiding the sun during the hottest part of the day and keeping indoor spaces cool are all things you can do to keep yourself and others safe. Business.title: Water companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect? | Nils Pratley
Business.summary: Door was left open to such behaviour because the regulator for England and Wales can only use the powers it was given by parliament Thames Water’s £1m payout to finance chief is ‘unacceptable’, says government department Anybody who followed the supposed “clampdown” on bankers’ bonuses after the great financial crash in 2008 knew what to expect when water company bosses became a similar target for a bash in the bonus department. We would see the waterbed principle in action: when you push down in one area of remuneration, such as the performance-related stuff, another tends to go up. Back in the day, banks invented “role-based allowances” – salary top-ups – to “compensate”, as they put it, their top earners for being subject to EU caps on bonuses. No executive was seriously inconvenienced by forgoing the chance of an astronomical (but not guaranteed) bonus and getting a smaller (but still hefty) increase in fixed pay instead. Some even preferred greater certainty over what they would take home. Continue reading...

Culture.title: The Galloping Cure review – powerful new opera tackles the opioid crisis with bite and black comedy
Culture.summary: Festival theatre, Edinburgh Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’s new music theatre work boasts a richly textured score with a direct but sophisticated musical language. Daniela Mack is ideal as the conflicted doctor as its heart Despite singing dogs and a chorus of hallucinogenic sheep, Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’s The Galloping Cure is not for the faint-hearted. Based on an original story by Karen Russell, itself inspired by Kafka’s A Country Doctor, the opera tells how a charismatic sideshow huckster rids a rural town of pain only to replace it with something far more sinister in a thinly veiled allegory of America’s opioid crisis. It’s a typically confronting slice of music theatre from the creators of Breaking the Waves , their acclaimed adaptation of Lars von Trier’s film. The plot centres on local doctor Theresa Hart and her efforts to cope with a community struggling with disillusionment and chronic illness. When a carnival arrives in town led by the mysterious Lucky Mack, the release people feel “flying” on his carousel (first ride is always free) seems like the answer to everyone’s prayers. At first Hart endorses the galloping cure, but Mack’s devious methods, including two-rides-a-week limits and surge pricing, lead to conflict, desperation and ultimately death. Contemporary parallels are a little obvious, but the opera nevertheless reflects the insidious way prescription painkillers affect ordinary people, elderly people and most tragically children.
